title: Ideals and absorption
section: Part B: Abstract Algebra ▷ Ring Homomorphisms
terms: ideal; two-sided ideal; left ideal; right ideal; principal ideal; ideal generated by elements.

exposition.text:
A two-sided ideal I in a ring R is an additive subgroup satisfying rI ⊆ I and Ir ⊆ I for every
r ∈ R. One-sided versions impose only one absorption condition. In a commutative unital ring,
the principal ideal (a) consists of multiples ra; (a, b) consists of sums ra + sb.
The kernel of a ring homomorphism is an ideal in the domain ring. An ideal in a unital ring
that contains 1, or any unit, equals the entire ring. A subring need not be an ideal, since clo-
sure under multiplication by its own members is weaker than absorption by all ambient ele-
ments. In Z, every ideal is nZ, and (a, b) = gcd(a, b)Z.
A left ideal requires rI ⊆ I for every ambient r; a right ideal requires Ir ⊆ I. In Z , every ideal
n
is generated by a divisor of n, and (a, b) is the set of multiples of gcd(n, a, b). In a full matrix
ring over a field, the only two-sided ideals are zero and the whole ring; multiplication on both
sides by matrix units proves this.

question.text:
What is the ideal of Z generated by 84 and 126?
(A) 6Z (B) 14Z (C) 21Z (D) 42Z (E) 252Z

solution.text:
Every integer combination is divisible by 42. Conversely 126 − 84 = 42, so all multiples of 42
lie in the generated ideal. Hence it is 42Z.

question.text:
Let D be the diagonal matrices in M (R). Which gives a valid proof that D is not a two-sided
2
ideal?
(A) D is not closed under addition.
(B) D is not closed under multiplication.
(C) D contains the identity but is a proper subset of the matrix ring.
(D) D contains the zero matrix.
(E) D is commutative.

solution.text:
A two-sided ideal containing I must contain every matrix A = AI. Diagonal matrices
form a proper subring containing I, so they cannot form an ideal. They are closed under
addition and multiplication; commutativity alone is not an obstruction to being an ideal.
